chicken-breast-grilled-with-sauce-skin-e.title: Chicken breast, grilled with sauce, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken breast is a lean, boneless cut of meat taken from the bird's chest. When grilled with sauce and the skin left on, it stays juicy while the flavorful sauce adds depth. Chicken is a widely consumed source of protein across many cultures.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken breast contains less fat than most other parts of the bird, but the skin adds a modest amount of healthy fats.
Grilling helps retain most nutrients while imparting a characteristic smoky aroma.
Sauces used for marinating often include herbs, spices, and a small amount of oil, enhancing flavor without dramatically increasing calories.
Chicken is a versatile base for dishes from Asian to Mediterranean cuisines.
Chicken breasts are a staple in sports nutrition due to their high protein and low carbohydrate content.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides about 31 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Skin‑less breast is virtually free of saturated fat; the skin adds only a modest amount of monounsaturated fats.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains niacin (B3), vitamin B6, and pyridoxine, which aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Chicken supplies phosphorus, selenium, and zinc, important for bones, immunity, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The high protein level and moderate fat help maintain a feeling of fullness longer.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Although rare, some individuals can have allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium in sauces
items.content: Prepared sauces are often high in salt; choose low‑sodium versions or make your own to control intake.

items.title: Skin adds calories
items.content: The skin increases calorie density and saturated fat content; those watching weight should consume it in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Grilled chicken breast with sauce and skin can be served as a main dish, sliced for salads, added to sandwiches, or tossed with pasta. Pair with vegetables, whole grains, or legumes for a balanced meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked breast in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in freezer‑safe bags for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken or turkey parmigiana is a baked dish made from poultry fillet topped with tomato sauce, melted cheese and breadcrumbs. It is traditionally served with pasta or vegetables. The turkey version is leaner, while the chicken version is more tender.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originates from Italian cuisine, where the classic version uses eggplant.
In Australia and the United States the chicken or turkey fillet is often substituted for the original eggplant.
Mozzarella and Parmesan give the dish its characteristic creamy and sharp flavor.
Tomato sauce can be made from fresh or canned tomatoes, making preparation convenient.
Parmigiana is frequently served as individual casseroles, ideal for family meals.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low fat content (turkey)
items.content: Turkey breast contains less saturated fat than chicken, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Poultry is high in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes supply lycopene, an antioxidant that helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus from cheese
items.content: The cheeses add calcium and phosphorus, important for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauce and cheeses often contain a lot of salt; individuals with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Possible pathogens in chicken
items.content: Undercooked chicken can harbor salmonella; ensure the internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A cheese‑topped casserole can be calorie‑rich; portion control is advisable for weight management.

content.title: How to Prepare and Serve
content.content: Dredge the fillet in flour, egg and breadcrumbs, pan‑fry until golden, then bake under tomato sauce topped with a mixture of mozzarella and Parmesan for 15‑20 minutes at 180 °C. Serve with pasta, rice or a fresh salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For freezing, place in a freezer‑safe bag and use within 2 months; reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Crème brûlée is a classic French dessert consisting of a baked custard topped with a caramelized sugar crust. Main ingredients are cream, egg yolks, sugar and vanilla. The dessert is known for its silky smooth texture and crisp caramel topping.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recorded recipe for crème brûlée appeared in France in the 17th century.
The word “brûlée” comes from the French verb “brûler,” meaning “to burn.”
Traditionally the crust is created with a kitchen torch, though a broiler can be used as well.
Variations exist worldwide: Spain has “flan,” Italy offers “panna cotta with caramel,” and many countries have their own take.
Crème brûlée is often served in small ramekins, which promote even cooking.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Cream and egg yolks provide calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Vitamin D
items.content: Cream contains vitamin D, which aids calcium absorption.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Egg yolks supply high‑quality protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The combination of fats and sugar offers a quick source of energy when consumed in moderation.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to tooth decay and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Cream makes the dessert rich in saturated fats, which may affect cholesterol levels.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: People allergic to eggs should avoid crème brûlée.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Crème brûlée is calorie‑dense, so portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve crème brûlée chilled, caramelizing the sugar crust just before serving. It can be garnished with berries, mint leaves, or a thin drizzle of chocolate. Eat with a spoon, gently cracking the crisp topping.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared crème brûlée keeps in the refrigerator in a sealed container for 2–3 days. Re‑caramelize the top with a torch or broiler before serving.

rice-brown-with-other-vegetables-no-adde.title: Brown Rice with Vegetables, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice with vegetables, no added fat is a whole‑grain rice dish cooked together with a mix of vegetables (such as carrots, broccoli, bell pepper) without using oil or other fats. The meal retains most of the nutrients from the rice and vegetables, providing a balanced source of carbohydrates, fiber, vitamins, and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice keeps the bran and germ, making it more nutritious than white rice.
Vegetables add not only flavor but also a wide range of phytochemicals beneficial for health.
Cooking without added fat allows precise calorie control and keeps saturated fat content low.
Brown rice has a lower glycemic index than white rice, helping to stabilize blood sugar levels.
The variety of vegetables boosts antioxidant content, including vitamin C and carotenoids.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Brown rice provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting digestive health and promoting satiety.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates deliver steady, lasting energy, which is important for active individuals.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from vegetables
items.content: The vegetables contribute vitamin A, vitamin C, folate, potassium, and magnesium, supporting immunity and heart function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes the dish suitable for low‑fat and calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Blood sugar regulation
items.content: The low glycemic index of brown rice combined with fiber helps prevent rapid glucose spikes.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce the absorption of certain minerals when consumed in very large amounts.

items.title: Food allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to specific vegetables (e.g., broccoli), potentially triggering allergic reactions.

items.title: Food safety with improper storage
items.content: If left at room temperature for more than 2 hours, the dish can become a breeding ground for bacteria.

items.title: Arsenic content
items.content: Brown rice may contain trace amounts of inorganic arsenic; it is advisable to vary grain sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish as a standalone meal or as a side to meat, fish, or tofu. It reheats well in the microwave or in a pan without added oil. For extra flavor, add fresh herbs, low‑sodium soy sauce, or a squeeze of lemon juice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked rice and vegetables in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions in freezer‑safe bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before eating.

rice-white-with-vegetables-and-gravy-no-.title: White Rice with Vegetables and Gravy, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: This dish consists of boiled white rice, a mix of vegetables (such as carrots, broccoli, peas) and a light gravy made from vegetable broth. It is prepared without any added oil or fat, making it low‑calorie and diet‑friendly.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is a staple carbohydrate source in many cultures.
Steaming vegetables preserves most of their vitamins and minerals.
Fat‑free gravies are often made from tomato puree, spices, and vegetable stock.
The dish can be easily customized by swapping different vegetables.
Properly cooked rice has a relatively low glycemic index.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice provides a quick source of energy through complex carbohydrates.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which support metabolism.

items.title: Fiber content
items.content: Vegetables add dietary fiber that aids healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes the meal suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish supplies potassium, magnesium, and phosphorus, important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Large portions of white rice can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to rice.

items.title: Lack of fats
items.content: Without dietary fat, the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins may be reduced if not compensated elsewhere in the diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish warm as a main course or as a side to lean meat or fish. Fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or a splash of soy sauce can enhance the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Store vegetables separately to prevent sogginess. When reheating, add a little water to restore moisture.
